title: Banjo lessons and joining Fate Marable's band on the Capitol
summary: Father bought him a banjo and Willie Foster taught him; then called to rehearse in St. Louis, arranging exams, and struggling to read the banjo book.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Well, before I had completed high school, my daddy bought me a banjo. Regular four string.
And I was being taught by Willie Foster, that's Pop Foster's brother. Oh yeah, I interviewed him up in Baton Rouge.
You did. About two years ago.
She was still living. She was 106 years old then. Yes. That's right. But had a stroke, so she couldn't talk.

And, uh, he taught me the banjo. For about a year and a half I was instructed by him. And he left to go to California. During that time he was playing on the Steamer Capitol. And, uh, through the friendship that existed between my father and fate, uh, I was given an opportunity to play on the Steamer Capitol. And they called me in for a rehearsal. I left them here on a Saturday and on that Sunday evening we had to rehearse in St. Louis on the boat.
Had you finished high school then about that time?

Yes, I had finished high school. I was in my first year of college. And, uh, the dean, Dean Hayes at the university arranged, it was near the final examination time. And he arranged, it was about three weeks prior to that time, and he arranged that I would take my examinations. And, uh, if I passed the examinations, it was decided between my mother, my parents, and he that if I passed that I would go. And if I didn't pass, well, I would have to remain. So, I went. And, uh, that Sunday evening I never will forget, but it called for rehearsal. And, uh, all of the band was naturally intact because they had been playing their repertoire. And they passed their banjo book to me. Well, I hadn't had any big band experience before. And most of the little bands that I had been, not most of them, but the one band particularly that I had been playing with before I went up there was Paul Mollier. I wanted to mention that in there. Have you heard of him?
I've heard of him. There's nothing about him though, actually.
Well, we'll get back to him.
I've heard of him just the mention.

I played with Paul Mollier's group. And, uh, they passed the book to me and started from the front of the book. It was, uh, during those years they didn't have the cymbals written over the chords that you play as a banjo player. You actually had to read the notes. Read the chords, yeah. And they were playing everything in the natural tempos that they were supposed to be played. And, uh, well, being frightened and being in a new environment, I just became frustrated. I didn't know what to do.
It's a tough thing to read that off its site.

And, uh, I didn't do so very good at the rehearsal. So the captain of the boat came up and asked, he said, what's the matter? He asked my dad, he said, what's wrong? He said, well he's nervous for one thing and then he's excited too. So he asked me, he said, is there anything that you feel that you can play at lib or you would like to play, to give me a general idea of how you play? So I said, well I can play Tiger Rag. And, uh, I played that. And the band played it in an up tempo. And, uh, I just went away with it. So he was very well pleased with what I had done then. And he said to the group then, he said, that this fellow has, this young fellow has a fine potential. And he expected the assistance from every man in the group in his spare time to help me. Because by the time we had completed the tour, we were going, we were leaving to go to St. Paul and then come back to New Orleans. He said that he expected to have me play many numbers as I had played Tiger Rag. Well it worked out just about that way. And, uh, when I came back to the band. Who else was in the band?
